BASTION decomposition with calendar seasonality

fit_BASTION_calendar.Rd

Bayesian trend and seasonal decomposition with locally adaptive priors.

Usage

fit_BASTION_calendar(y, dates, data_unit, seasonalities, X = NULL,
  Outlier = FALSE, cl = .95, sparse = FALSE, obsSV = "const",
  nchains = 2L, nsave = 1000L, nburn = 1000L, nskip = 4L,
  verbose = TRUE, save_samples = FALSE, D_trend = 2L,
  tz = NULL, tolerance_seconds = NULL, deviation_periods = NULL)

Arguments

y

Numeric observations; NA allowed.

dates

POSIXct timestamps matching the observations.

data_unit

Collection interval list with unit, optional every and anchor.

seasonalities

Named seasonal specification lists with unit, optional every, anchor and distance_scale.

X

Optional regression design matrix.

Outlier

Include outliers with a horseshoe+ prior at all observations (default FALSE).

cl

Pointwise equal-tailed credible interval probability.

sparse

Additional trend shrinkage option; not a matrix storage switch.

obsSV

Observation variance model: "const" or "SV".

nchains

Number of chains.

nsave

Saved draws per chain.

nburn

Burn-in sweeps per chain.

nskip

Discarded sweeps between saves; save every nskip+1 sweeps.

verbose

Display progress.

save_samples

Return posterior draws.

D_trend

Trend difference order, 1 or 2 (default 2).

tz

Optional explicit time zone.

tolerance_seconds

Timestamp matching tolerance passed to preprocessing.

deviation_periods

Optional named fixed-lag overrides. Supply these for modal ties or no complete cycles.

Details

BASTION decomposes a time series into a locally adaptive trend, one or more seasonal components, and optional regression and outlier components. The calendar fitter uses observation dates to align seasonal patterns with calendar cycles. All components are estimated jointly using Bayesian inference.

Supply observations through y and matching POSIXct timestamps through dates. Use data_unit to describe the observation interval, such as list(unit = "day") for daily data or list(unit = "hour") for hourly data.

Specify seasonal patterns as a named list through seasonalities. For example, list(weekly = list(unit = "week"), yearly = list(unit = "year")) fits weekly and yearly seasonality together. Calendar alignment accommodates different cycle lengths, such as months with different numbers of days and leap years. Each seasonal component combines a smooth recurring pattern with deviations that allow the pattern to evolve across cycles.

The trend uses second differences by default (D_trend = 2). Use D_trend = 1 for first differences. Setting sparse = TRUE applies stronger shrinkage to trend differences while retaining local adaptivity.

Use obsSV = "const" for constant observation variance or obsSV = "SV" to estimate observation variability over time. Set Outlier = TRUE to estimate a separate outlier component, and supply X to include regression effects.

Missing observations are estimated during fitting. The returned timeline includes all scheduled timestamps, and imputation identifies those with missing observations. Component estimates and observation standard deviations are returned in the units of the supplied data. Posterior means and credible intervals at the level specified by cl are returned whether or not posterior draws are retained. Set save_samples = TRUE to retain the draws.

Use print() for an overview of the fit, summary() for the component estimates, plot() for the decomposition, and plot_component() to inspect an individual component with credible intervals. Seasonal component names follow the names supplied in seasonalities, such as seasonal_weekly and seasonal_yearly.

Value

An object of class bastion_fit, with the same component, interval, seasonality, regression, noise and optional draw structure as fit_BASTION. Let T be all scheduled timestamps, D saved draws, M decomposition columns (including residual), J native phase-grid positions, and H missing collection slots.

time, observed

All scheduled timestamps in chronological order with the resolved time zone, and observations, length T. Missing responses are NA, including omitted timestamps.

components

T by M posterior-mean data frame, with trend, seasonal_<supplied name>, regression/outlier when fitted, and residual.

intervals

T by M lower and upper data frames with matching component names/order.

seasonality

Each named entry has recurring, a J by 3 data frame (mean, lower, upper), and deviation, a T by 3 data frame (mean, lower, upper). Native phase coordinates in [0,1) are stored in metadata$mapping$recurring_positions.

regression

Optional coefficient summaries, as in fit_BASTION.

noise

SD summaries and SV parameter summaries when applicable, as in fit_BASTION. Residuals are included in components and intervals.

metadata

Fitting metadata includes cl, the credible-interval probability, and alpha = 1 - cl. Input specifications (including collection unit/anchor and time zone), fitting arguments, and compact seasonality mappings under mapping$seasonality. Each seasonality has its unit, every, anchor, phase_index (length T), pattern_id (length T), and patterns (a list of full-cycle grid-index vectors). These indices refer to rows of its recurring table.

imputation

POSIXct vector of H timestamps with missing responses, including explicit missing responses and omitted collection timestamps. All component estimates and intervals remain on the full timeline.

draws

Only when save_samples=TRUE. Components are D by T by M; recurring patterns D by J; deviations are D by T, and residuals are included in the component array. Noise SD is D by T under SV or D by 1 otherwise; SV parameters are D by 3. Regression coefficients and draw/chain/iteration indices follow fit_BASTION. Completed-response draws can be recovered by summing components, including residual, within each draw.

Supplying observation dates and intervals

y must be a numeric vector, and dates must be a POSIXct vector of the same length, with a valid time zone. Each timestamp identifies the observation in the corresponding position of y. Convert character dates before calling the fitter, for example with as.POSIXct(date_text, tz = "UTC").

data_unit describes how often observations are collected. Supply a list containing unit and, optionally, every and anchor. For example, list(unit = "day") means one observation per day, list(unit = "day", every = 2) means one observation every two days, and list(unit = "minute", every = 15) means one observation every 15 minutes. The default value of every is 1.

Use the intended observation interval even when some observations are missing. For daily data with missing days, keep data_unit = list(unit = "day"). Missing responses may be supplied as NA; omitted timestamps are also recognized as missing positions in that interval. If X is supplied, include every timestamp and its covariates, using NA in y for missing responses.

Allowed units are "millisecond", "second", "minute", "hour", "day", "week", "month", "quarter", and "year". Day, week, month, quarter, and year use calendar intervals and require a positive integer every. Subdaily units use elapsed time and allow positive fractional values, such as list(unit = "second", every = 0.01) for observations every 10 milliseconds.

Specifying seasonal patterns

seasonalities is a named list with one list per seasonal component. Each component has unit, optional every (default 1), optional anchor, and optional distance_scale (default TRUE). The allowed units are the same as for data_unit. The list names label the results; for example, biweekly = list(unit = "week", every = 2) creates a component named seasonal_biweekly.

Here unit and every describe how often a seasonal pattern repeats. With daily observations, list(unit = "week") repeats every week, list(unit = "week", every = 2) repeats every two weeks, and list(unit = "month") repeats every calendar month. With hourly observations, list(unit = "day") repeats every day. Supplying multiple entries estimates those seasonal components together.

Keep the observation interval and the seasonal period separate: daily observations with a biweekly pattern use data_unit = list(unit = "day") and seasonalities = list(biweekly = list(unit = "week", every = 2)). The seasonal cycle must contain enough observations to estimate its shape; a daily pattern cannot be estimated from one observation per day.

anchor sets a reference boundary for an interval or seasonal cycle and must be a single POSIXct timestamp. The observation interval defaults to the earliest supplied timestamp. Seasonal boundaries default to midnight on January 1, 1970, except weekly cycles use Monday, January 5, 1970, in the selected time zone. For a two-week cycle, set a custom anchor to specify which week starts the cycle.

distance_scale = TRUE accounts for spacing between seasonal positions when smoothing a grid-based recurring pattern. Set it to FALSE to use unscaled second differences for that pattern. This option is supplied separately within each seasonal specification; it does not change the observation interval or the number of days in a calendar cycle.

See also

simulate_BASTION_calendar

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Daily observations with weekly and yearly patterns
sim <- simulate_BASTION_calendar("daily", seed = 20)
fit_daily <- fit_BASTION_calendar(
  y = sim$y,
  dates = sim$dates,
  data_unit = list(unit = "day"),
  seasonalities = list(
    weekly = list(unit = "week"),
    yearly = list(unit = "year")
  ),
  obsSV = "const", nchains = 1
)
plot(fit_daily)

# Daily observations; the pattern repeats every two weeks
sim <- simulate_BASTION_calendar("biweekly", seed = 21)
fit_biweekly <- fit_BASTION_calendar(
  y = sim$y,
  dates = sim$dates,
  data_unit = list(unit = "day"),
  seasonalities = list(
    biweekly = list(unit = "week", every = 2, anchor = sim$dates[1])
  ),
  obsSV = "const", nchains = 1
)
plot_component(fit_biweekly, "seasonal_biweekly")

# Hourly observations with daily and weekly patterns
sim <- simulate_BASTION_calendar("hourly", seed = 22)
fit_hourly <- fit_BASTION_calendar(
  y = sim$y,
  dates = sim$dates,
  data_unit = list(unit = "hour"),
  seasonalities = list(
    daily = list(unit = "day"),
    weekly = list(unit = "week")
  ),
  obsSV = "const", nchains = 1
)
plot(fit_hourly)
} # }
